title: Seretse and Ruth Khama Defy Two Governments
text:
Seretse Khama was the heir to the chieftainship of the Bamangwato, the largest people of the British protectorate of Bechuanaland. While studying law in London after the Second World War, he met Ruth Williams, an English office clerk. They married in September 1948.

The marriage set off a crisis. Seretse's uncle, Tshekedi Khama, who had ruled as regent during his youth, opposed it. Next door, South Africa had just elected the National Party, which was building apartheid and soon outlawed mixed marriages. South Africa and Southern Rhodesia pressed Britain not to accept a chief with a white wife. Britain depended on South Africa for gold and uranium. A British judicial inquiry found that Seretse was fit to rule, but the government kept its report secret. In 1950 it banished him from his own country.

Ruth stood by him. Their first child, Jacqueline, was born in Serowe while the dispute raged, and the couple spent the exile years in England. The Bamangwato repeatedly asked for his return. In 1956 Seretse and Ruth were allowed back, after he renounced his claim to the chieftainship.

He entered politics instead. When Bechuanaland became independent as Botswana in 1966, Seretse Khama was elected its first president, and he was knighted the same year. Ruth became the First Lady. Their son Ian Khama later became president too.
lesson: A marriage can hold firm against pressure from governments as well as families. What others forbid may become, with patience, the foundation of a new life.
people: Seretse Khama, Ruth Williams Khama, Tshekedi Khama
source: Susan Williams, Colour Bar: The Triumph of Seretse Khama and His Nation (2006); British government records
